title: Chinese Court Orders $34,000 Payout After Wedding Prank Leaves Bridesmaid With Fractured Spine
excerpt: A 20-year-old woman was left permanently disabled when groomsmen tossed her in a bedsheet during a traditional hazing ritual, reigniting debate over dangerous wedding customs across Asia.
body:
• A 20-year-old bridesmaid named Zhang suffered a burst fracture of her first lumbar vertebra after groomsmen threw her into the air using a bedsheet during a wedding in October 2023
  • A Chinese court ordered the wedding party to pay approximately $34,000 (Rs 28.5 lakh) in compensation, holding the newlyweds liable for 40% of the damages
  • Zhang was diagnosed with Grade 9 disability, corresponding to a 20% permanent disability rate, after 18 days in hospital
  • The case has renewed scrutiny of hunnao, a centuries-old Chinese wedding hazing tradition that has drawn criticism for escalating into violence

A court in China has ordered a wedding party to pay nearly $34,000 in compensation after a bridesmaid suffered a fractured spine during a traditional wedding prank that left her permanently disabled.

The incident occurred in October 2023 when Zhang, a 20-year-old woman, served as a bridesmaid at a close friend's wedding, according to court documents obtained by the South China Morning Post, the Global Times, and the Yangtze Evening Post.

What Happened in the Wedding Room

Zhang was left alone in a wedding room with 10 men, most of them groomsmen, as part of hunnao, an ancient Chinese custom originally meant to ward off evil spirits and break the ice for newlyweds. The tradition has evolved over time into what often manifests as aggressive and dangerous pranks directed at bridesmaids and the couple.

"On the second attempt, she fell to the floor.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"><p>"He pulled her onto the bed, and the others grabbed the corners of the blanket and threw it up."

According to court documents, one groomsman dragged Zhang out of a closet where she was hiding and pushed her onto a bed. He and the other men then held the corners of a bedsheet and tossed her into the air. They caught her the first time. On the second attempt, she fell to the floor.

"He pulled her onto the bed, and the others grabbed the corners of the blanket and threw it up. A total of 10 people participated in pulling the blanket; I didn’t recognize the others."

— Groomsman Hu, court testimony via Yangtze Evening Post

Hu, one of the groomsmen who testified that he did not participate in the hazing, carried Zhang downstairs to wait for an ambulance, according to People magazine.

Permanent Disability at 20

Zhang was hospitalized for 18 days and diagnosed with a burst fracture of her first lumbar vertebra. A judicial appraisal later determined her injury constituted a Grade 9 disability under China's classification system, corresponding to a 20% permanent disability rate.

She sued the newlyweds and the nine individuals involved, seeking approximately $40,000 in compensation for medical expenses and emotional distress.

Court Assigns Shared Liability

The court held the newlyweds responsible for 40% of the compensation, ruling that they had failed to take effective measures to stop the pranks despite being aware of the local custom. The groomsman who dragged Zhang from the closet bore 20% of the liability, and the remaining eight participants jointly covered the final 40%. The total award came to nearly $34,000.

A Problem Beyond China

The case has reignited public debate over hunnao and similar wedding hazing traditions across Asia. While originally ceremonial, these customs have been linked to injuries and deaths in recent years. In 2016, three men in southwestern China were ordered to pay over 100,000 yuan after tying up a groom, causing injuries that left him permanently disabled.

The issue resonates beyond China. Wedding pranks have been a subject of concern in India as well, where elaborate rituals during ceremonies have occasionally resulted in accidents and injuries. The case underscores the tension between cultural tradition and personal safety, a conversation that continues to evolve across the region.
